title: ⭐ Practice: naming what a mind can do

questions.prompt: One set of the questionnaire asks: "Do you feel active and full of energy? Do you enjoy sport? Can you express your feelings by gestures?" Which type of intelligence is that set about?
questions.explanation: "physical" is the type: energy, sport and feelings shown with the body are its three signs, and the set carries one in every question. "artistic" is the near miss, because it too is about expressing something, but it goes through words or pictures — a story, a poem, a drawing — never through a gesture. "social" would need somebody else to understand or to listen to, and "creative" something invented that did not exist before. Read the three questions of the set together before you choose.

questions.prompt: Complete: "Nobody ever taught Nadia the oud, and she has played it since she was five. Music is her ___."
questions.explanation: "gift" fills the gap: a gift is the ability itself, a noun, and here it is what Nadia owns — nobody taught it to her. "gifted" is the adjective and needs another sentence around it: Nadia is gifted at music. "prodigy" names a young person, not an ability, so music cannot be her prodigy, and "brain" names the organ she thinks with, not what that organ can do.

questions.prompt: Complete: "Sleep is not lost time: while you sleep, your ___ sorts out everything you learned during the day."
questions.explanation: "brain" fills the gap: it names the organ, the thing that does the work, and filing away a day of lessons is work. "curiosity" is the wish that made you learn in the morning, not the machine that sorts it out at night. "gift" is an ability the brain makes possible, not the organ, and "remarkable" is an adjective: it can describe the night's work, it cannot do it.

questions.prompt: One line of the model poem is "Undertaking projects". What does undertake mean there?

options.text: to take a project away from a partner
to take something out from under a table
to work under the orders of somebody else in a firm
to begin a piece of work and take charge of it

questions.explanation: "to begin a piece of work and take charge of it" is the meaning: the pupil of the poem starts the project and carries it himself. "to take something out from under a table" and "to work under the orders of somebody else in a firm" both read the two halves of the word separately, which is the trap. "to take a project away from a partner" would need a verb of taking from, and the poem describes what a pupil does, not what he steals.

questions.prompt: Your partner reads your draft and writes: "Everything in your description is nice: a nice boy, a nice voice, a nice family. Find other words." Which of the three points is he correcting?
questions.explanation: "the vocabulary" is the point: a remark about which words you chose, and about repeating one of them, is a remark on your stock of words. "the grammar" would be about a wrong form, and "the ideas" about something you say or fail to say. "the spelling of the words" is not one of the three points the lesson asks a partner to look at.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The way he repairs an engine with only two tools is ___: everybody in the garage comes to look."
questions.explanation: "remarkable" is right: the gap follows is and describes the way he works, so an adjective is needed, and remarkable means so good that people notice it — here the whole garage does. "remarkably" is the adverb and would have to sit next to another adjective. "remark" and "remarked" belong to the verb to remark, which means to notice or to say, and neither of them can describe a way of working.
